name: Mandarin Orange
lede: Mandarin Orange is a deep, reddish orange named for the fruit; a dictionary calls the name a reddish yellow, and the exact tone has drifted.

notes.cite: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, "Mandarin orange"
ColorHub library (data/library.json): Maerz & Paul 1930 pl. 11 B 12 (first recorded 1883); CIEDE2000
ColorHub archive field notes for Mandarin Orange (n=137), 23,781 museum paintings as photographed; data/graph/fieldnotes/m.json

sections.title: A fruit and a dye name
sections.body: Paterson defines Mandarin as a strong yellow and Mandarin orange as a reddish yellow, adding Mandarin red as a variant [1]. The swatch here is darker and redder than that, a burnt orange, so the dictionary's tone is lighter than this page's [2]. The books read do not trace the name's origin beyond the fruit [1]. Finlay lists a mandarin garnet, an orange stone from Namibia and Pakistan, so the word also names a gem [3].

sections.title: On the old charts
sections.body: The library finds the color only in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, which first records the name in 1883 on plate 11 B 12, and files it under fashion and textiles [2]. The nearest everyday name is [[orange]], about eight units away; close neighbors are [[tangerine]] and [[burnt-orange]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is fairly common in museum paintings: 137 of 23,781 contain it, about 0.58 per cent, more common than 62 per cent of our named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1700s at 0.8 per cent of paintings, 1.4 times the expected rate [4]. Inside a painting it is an accent in 90 per cent of the 121 paintings measured [4].
